extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in entertainment, culture, and #MeToo-era accountability
extracted.subtask_description: A short-form news feature describing a public apology by a celebrity/industry figure and the response, highlighting what made the apology effective or problematic. Focuses on narrative, quotes, context, and public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give a full, specific account of the wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmon gave a full account of how and when he harassed Ganz, describing attraction, specific behaviors, timeline and context (e.g., while working together, breakup, his actions afterward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concrete about what you did — avoid vagueness. A detailed, honest narrative (as Harmon did on a seven-minute podcast) helps make the apology believable and allows listeners to understand the scope of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge power dynamics and impact on the victim
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmon recognized the 'tricky power dynamic' of being in a position of authority and admitted his actions damaged Ganz's 'internal compass' and ability to evaluate her talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly name how power, position, or authority contributed to the misconduct and the specific harms (career, self-confidence) inflicted on the victim; this demonstrates awareness beyond abstract remorse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept responsibility without excuses or deflection
rubrics_metrics.description: He said he was 'deeply sorry' and called himself 'an awful boss and selfish baby,' taking responsibility rather than minimizing or blaming circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear language of culpability; avoid conditional language ('if I offended') or explanations that shift blame. Own the behavior plainly and avoid minimizing phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not burden the victim with instructing your redemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes criticism that Harmon initially burdened Ganz by asking her to tell him 'how to fix it,' which many condemned as placing the labor of remediation on the victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asking the harmed person to coach or educate you about how to be forgiven; seek guidance elsewhere (trusted peers, professional advisors) so the victim does not bear remediation labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek and heed advice from respected peers (especially women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmon credited advice from women he respected who told him to publicly discuss how he'd been part of the problem; he followed that counsel in making his apology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult sincere, informed peers (particularly those from groups affected) and act on their guidance. Demonstrating that you've listened to counsel — and did the hard work of speaking publicly — supports credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent/public when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmon apologized publicly on his podcast and Ganz accepted publicly on social media; the article frames public transparency as part of the apology's effectiveness in the #MeToo context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public apologies can be appropriate when the harm was public or systemic, and when transparency aids accountability. However, balance publicness with victim privacy/preferences and avoid performative displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge consequences and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmon referenced concrete consequences (Sony Television fired him in 2012, he 'lost my job,' 'ruined my show'), signaling that his actions had real costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioning or accepting consequences — institutional or personal — signals accountability. Where possible, support remediation with concrete steps or accepting institutional outcomes rather than claiming innocence or minimizing consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the victim's agency in forgiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ganz chose to listen and later publicly accept the apology; she wrote that forgiveness, if done, should be done 'in the light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forgiveness is the harmed person's decision. Do not demand or presume forgiveness; allow the victim to set the terms and timeline, and respect their public or private choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use apology as a prompt for broader reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmon ended by imploring listeners to think about their own actions at work, turning a personal apology into a call for communal introspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologies can include a commitment to change and a call for others to examine behavior. This helps link individual accountability to cultural or organizational change, but should not replace individual responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and sincerity matter — late apologies can still be meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: Ganz waited six years for an apology; the article emphasizes that, although delayed, the apology provided relief when it was sincere and thorough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While prompt apologies are preferable, delayed apologies may still be valuable if they are sincere, specific, and accompanied by acknowledgement of harm and accountability. Don't use lateness as an excuse for lack of substance.
